title: App Intents is the only door into an app — and no app may open another app's door
what_is_allowed: A third-party app declares AppIntent structs to EXPOSE its own actions. Only the system (Siri/Apple Intelligence, Spotlight, Shortcuts, widgets, Control Center, Focus filters) discovers and invokes them. At WWDC 2026 (June 9) Apple deprecated SiriKit outright, making App Intents the sole path by which Siri reaches a third-party app; apps without App Intents are dropped from Siri's multi-app compositions and lose Spotlight indexing.
what_is_forbidden: There is no public API for one application to invoke another application's App Intent. App-to-app reach is limited to URL schemes / universal links, which open the target app to the foreground and hand control to the user. An agent app cannot programmatically drive a third-party app's intent graph.
why_it_matters: On iOS your assistant can be a callable tool for Apple's orchestrator, but it can never be the orchestrator itself.

title: Siri AI composes multi-app workflows from third-party App Intents
what_is_allowed: Apps that publish App Intents become components in Siri's agentic compositions — Siri determines which app capability completes each step and invokes them in sequence (e.g. summarize an email, reserve a restaurant, send an itinerary). App Intents 2.0 adds richer entity types, streaming responses for long-running actions, multi-turn follow-ups, and a View Annotations API so users can reference on-screen elements by voice.
what_is_forbidden: The composing agent is Siri, not your app. Third-party apps never see other apps' data; all personal-context resolution happens on-device or in Private Cloud Compute and is not exposed to app code. Your app only ever receives the parameters for its own intent.
why_it_matters: Cross-app action on iOS is a privilege Apple reserves for itself — the best a third party can do is be an excellent tool that Siri picks up.

title: iOS 27 LongRunningIntent breaks the 30-second background intent ceiling
what_is_allowed: An App Intent invoked by Siri can now run in the background without bringing the app to the foreground, and `LongRunningIntent` extends the historical ~30-second budget for file I/O, sync, and on-device ML inference via `performBackgroundTask(options:operation:)`. Progress feeds directly into a Lock Screen Live Activity.
what_is_forbidden: The extension is conditional: `LongRunningIntent` requires conformance to `ProgressReportingIntent` — you cannot take the long-running budget without continuously reporting progress, and the system revokes the extension and kills the task if reporting stops. Some operations still force foreground via `IntentExecutionTargets`. Crucially, this budget is only granted on user invocation, not on the app's own initiative.
why_it_matters: Long background reasoning is now possible on iOS, but only downstream of a user asking — it is an extension of a user turn, not self-directed autonomy.

title: Guideline 2.5.11: you may only register intents your own app can fulfil
what_is_allowed: Registering intents for functionality your app performs itself, resolving the request in the most direct way possible.
what_is_forbidden: Verbatim: 'Apps integrating SiriKit and Shortcuts should only sign up for intents they can handle without the support of an additional app and that users would expect from the stated functionality.' Aliases 'must relate directly to your app or company name and should not be generic terms or include third-party app names or services.' No ads or marketing may be inserted between the request and its fulfilment.
why_it_matters: This is the explicit App Review rule that blocks a generic 'do anything across my apps' assistant from registering itself as the handler for everything.

title: Guidelines 2.5.2 and 2.5.9: no reaching outside your container, no altering other apps
what_is_allowed: Operating inside your own sandbox container using public APIs for their intended purpose (2.5.1).
what_is_forbidden: 2.5.2 verbatim: apps 'may not read or write data outside the designated container area, nor may they download, install, or execute code which introduces or changes features or functionality of the app, including other apps.' 2.5.9: apps that 'alter or disable the functions of standard switches... or other native user interface elements or behaviors will be rejected... apps should not block links out to other apps or other features that users would expect to work a certain way.'
why_it_matters: Even if a clever technique existed to script another iOS app, shipping it is a guideline rejection, not a grey area.

title: Guideline 5.1.2(i): explicit in-app consent before any personal data reaches a third-party AI
what_is_allowed: Sending user data to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral or your own hosted model — after you name the provider, explain what it will do with the data, and capture explicit consent in a visible in-app prompt.
what_is_forbidden: Relying on a privacy-policy link is no longer sufficient. The consent prompt must appear BEFORE the first transmission; reviewers test on a fresh install and if the API call to the third-party AI fires before the consent screen, rejection is automatic. Live since 2025-11-13 with consistent enforcement through 2026.
why_it_matters: A proactive assistant that quietly streams calendar/contact context to a cloud model in the background is an automatic rejection unless consent is gated up front.

title: Messages: no programmatic send, no read access, no contact-recency signal
what_is_allowed: Presenting `MFMessageComposeViewController` pre-filled with recipients and body; the user reads it and taps Send. An app may register as an SMS spam filter extension, which sees only incoming messages from unknown numbers.
what_is_forbidden: There is no API to send SMS/iMessage programmatically or in the background. Third-party apps have zero read access to the Messages database — you cannot read, export, or save SMS/iMessage history, and the spam-filter extension may not save or export what it sees. The Contacts framework exposes no last-contacted, creation, or modification date, so 'who did I talk to most recently' is not derivable from system data.
why_it_matters: The single most valuable proactive action — 'I noticed you haven't replied to X, want me to send this?' — cannot be completed without a human tap, and the trigger signal itself is unavailable.

title: Screen Time API returns opaque tokens and runs in a network-less extension
what_is_allowed: FamilyControls requests authorization and presents a FamilyActivityPicker; ManagedSettings applies OS-enforced shields/blocks; DeviceActivity schedules windows and fires threshold events (e.g. 30 minutes on an app today). Usage can be rendered to the user inside a DeviceActivityReport SwiftUI extension.
what_is_forbidden: Apple never shows the developer the user's usage data — app identities arrive as opaque tokens you cannot resolve to bundle IDs, and the report extension is sandboxed with no network access, so usage figures cannot be exfiltrated to your backend for reasoning. Enforcement is performed by the OS, not your app.
why_it_matters: You can build attention interventions on iOS but you cannot build a server-side model of how the user actually spends their day.

title: HealthKit background delivery is one of the few legitimate self-wake triggers
what_is_allowed: Per-type read and write authorization across health and workout data. `HKObserverQuery` combined with `enableBackgroundDelivery` wakes the app in the background when new samples arrive, with a frequency parameter of immediate / hourly / daily; `HKAnchoredObjectQuery` then fetches only what's new. Apps may also write samples and workouts.
what_is_forbidden: Frequency is capped per data type (most types are hourly or daily, not immediate), the user controls each type independently and read denial is indistinguishable from 'no data', and the wake is event-driven — it is not a general-purpose scheduler for arbitrary reasoning.
why_it_matters: Health events are the most reliable way to get CPU time on iOS without the user opening your app, which makes them the natural spine of a proactive assistant's daily loop.

title: Live Activities: remotely started, remotely updated, interactive — now policed by 4.5.3
what_is_allowed: ActivityKit lets a server remotely start, update, and end a Live Activity via push tokens. Buttons and toggles inside a Live Activity or widget run a `LiveActivityIntent` / `AppIntent` in the background without opening the app. Live Activities surface on Lock Screen, Dynamic Island, iPad, Apple Watch and Mac.
what_is_forbidden: New guideline 4.5.3 (added in the June 9, 2026 update) forbids using Apple services including Live Activities to 'spam, phish, or send unsolicited messages to customers'. A Live Activity must reflect a real, time-sensitive, user-relevant event — deliveries, rides, timers, workouts, scores, travel, active sessions — and may not act as a second promotional notification channel. Push notifications may not be required for the app to function.
why_it_matters: This is the richest proactive surface a third-party app owns outright — and the 2026 rule change means a 'here's your day' ambient Live Activity with no underlying live event is now a rejection risk.

title: Shortcuts personal automations can run silently — but only the user can create them
what_is_allowed: The USER, in the Shortcuts app, can create a personal automation on a time, location, charger, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, Focus-change or CarPlay trigger, turn off 'Ask Before Running' (confirming 'Don't Ask') and 'Notify When Run', and have it fire with no tap and no banner. Such an automation can call your app's App Intents.
what_is_forbidden: There is no API for an app to programmatically install, enable, or silently modify a personal automation — you can offer a shortcut for the user to add, but they perform the setup and the 'Don't Ask' confirmation themselves. Sensitive actions (sending messages, payments, deleting data) still surface a confirmation tap by design, and NFC and some location triggers still surface a notification you must tap even with Ask Before Running off.
why_it_matters: The one genuinely unattended automation path on iOS requires a multi-step manual user setup you cannot script, which caps its realistic adoption at power users.

title: Focus filters let an app change its own behaviour when the user's Focus changes
what_is_allowed: Implementing `SetFocusFilterIntent` lets the user bind per-Focus configuration to your app (e.g. which account/inbox/persona is active in Work vs Personal), and your `perform()` is called by the system on Focus change so the app reconfigures itself without being opened.
what_is_forbidden: A Focus filter only reconfigures YOUR app. It cannot read or alter other apps' Focus behaviour, cannot enumerate the user's Focus modes arbitrarily, and cannot set the device Focus on the user's behalf. (Reported broken/flaky on recent macOS 26.5 and iOS 18 betas, with conforming to LiveActivityIntent as a known workaround.)
why_it_matters: Focus is the only first-class 'what mode is this person in right now' signal an app can subscribe to, which makes it the cheapest real context source for proactivity.

title: BGTaskScheduler is opportunistic — an app cannot reliably wake itself to think
what_is_allowed: Scheduling background work: `BGAppRefreshTask` for short content refreshes and `BGProcessingTask` for longer idle-time work (requires explicit entitlement plus power/connectivity conditions); iOS 26 adds a user-initiated continuation task.
what_is_forbidden: A total of only 1 refresh task and 10 processing tasks may be scheduled at any time, and run time is opportunistic and not guaranteed. iOS decides frequency from how often the user opens the app, battery, time of day, network reachability and thermal state. Heavily used apps may get several runs a day; rarely used apps may get one a week — or none at all if the user recently force-quit the app, which suppresses background refresh entirely.
why_it_matters: The core premise of 'my assistant wakes up and reasons about my day' has no guaranteed execution substrate on iOS — it degrades to zero for exactly the users who haven't opened the app.

title: Foundation Models 2026: vision on-device, 4K context locally, 32K on Private Cloud Compute
what_is_allowed: A native Swift API over a hybrid stack — the on-device Apple model (now accepting image input, with better instruction following), Apple server models on Private Cloud Compute, and third-party frontier models (Claude, Gemini) behind one session API. Adds agentic primitives, Dynamic Profiles for changing model behaviour on the fly, custom skills, a Python SDK, CLI and evals framework; going open source including on Linux.
what_is_forbidden: The on-device context window is 4096 tokens SHARED across input and output; Private Cloud Compute raises it only to 32K, also a shared budget. That is a hard ceiling on how much of a person's day can be reasoned over in one pass locally.
why_it_matters: Free local inference is real, but 4K shared context means a personal assistant must aggressively summarize and retrieve rather than hold the user's life in context.

title: Private Cloud Compute at zero cloud API cost for small developers
what_is_allowed: Developers enrolled in the App Store Small Business Program whose apps have fewer than 2 million first-time App Store downloads in total can run the next generation of Apple Foundation Models on Private Cloud Compute at no cloud API cost.
what_is_forbidden: Apple's newsroom announcement does not publish rate limits, per-user quotas, or overage terms; eligibility is tied to Small Business Program enrolment and the 2M lifetime-download threshold, so the free tier ends exactly when a consumer app succeeds. PCC context remains 32K shared.
why_it_matters: This removes the per-token margin trap for a pre-scale consumer assistant, and because nothing leaves Apple's stack it also sidesteps the 5.1.2(i) third-party-AI consent prompt.

title: AccessibilityService: autonomous agents are explicitly banned, static scripts are not
what_is_allowed: Verbatim carve-out: 'deterministic, rule-based automation, where behavior follows a static, human-defined script' is permitted. Genuine accessibility tools declaring `isAccessibilityTool="true"` (screen readers, switch access, voice input, Braille) may use the API for autonomous functionality in service of assisting people with disabilities. Non-accessibility apps must pass the Permission Declaration Form, show prominent in-app disclosure during normal usage (not buried in a menu) with affirmative consent, and submit a video.
what_is_forbidden: Verbatim: Google Play forbids 'use of the Accessibility API that enables an app to autonomously initiate, plan, and execute actions or decisions.' Explicitly ineligible categories: 'antivirus software, automation tools, assistants, monitoring apps, cleaners, password managers, and launchers.' The policy directly targets automation flows that navigate apps, LLM agents that book/buy/message/change settings, 'do it for me' assistants, and UI-driving RPA tools. Deceptive use results in app suspension and/or developer account termination. Enforcement from 2026-01-28.
why_it_matters: This is the single rule that decides the question: an LLM planning and executing steps across other Android apps via accessibility is a policy violation by definition, no matter how well it works.

title: Android 17 Advanced Protection auto-revokes accessibility from anything not an accessibility tool
what_is_allowed: Apps declaring `isAccessibilityTool="true"` and classified as screen readers, switch-based input, voice-based input, or Braille access keep AccessibilityService access with Advanced Protection Mode on.
what_is_forbidden: With Advanced Protection Mode enabled on Android 17 (stable 2026-06-16), the OS scans installed apps and automatically revokes AccessibilityService access from any app not classified as an accessibility tool, and blocks granting it in future. There is no per-app override — the user must disable Advanced Protection Mode entirely. Tasker and comparable automation tools were revoked. Android 16, including latest QPR builds, leaves accessibility alone.
why_it_matters: Even the grey-market accessibility-driven agent now breaks silently on a growing slice of devices, turning a policy risk into a runtime reliability problem.

title: AppFunctions: the sanctioned cross-app action API — but gated to approved callers
what_is_allowed: AppFunctions is an Android platform API plus Jetpack library that turns apps into on-device MCP-style servers exposing structured, typed functions as tools for agents. Execution is local, structured, and does not simulate taps or read the screen. Callers 'must have the EXECUTE_APP_FUNCTIONS permission to discover and execute AppFunctions, and can include agents, apps, and AI assistants like Gemini.' Requires Android 16+. Uber, DoorDash and OpenTable have shipped integrations.
what_is_forbidden: The API is in an experimental preview and 'subject to change'. As of 2026, Gemini integration is a private preview limited to trusted testers, and only a limited number of apps and system agents can access the end-to-end pipeline — access is via an Early Access Program. EXECUTE_APP_FUNCTIONS is a restricted permission, not something a consumer app simply declares and ships.
why_it_matters: This is the only legitimate route to real cross-app action on a stock phone, and in 2026 it is an invite-list, not a public capability.

title: SEND_SMS and CALL_PHONE are reserved for default handlers
what_is_allowed: An app actively registered as the DEFAULT SMS, Phone, or Assistant handler may request SMS/Call Log permission groups, limited strictly to documented core functionality essential to the app's primary purpose, and must stop using the permission the moment it loses default-handler status. Any app may fire an Intent to hand a pre-filled message or dial to the user's default app.
what_is_forbidden: 'Any other apps, regardless of their purpose, will be unable to request permission.' Data obtained may never be used for advertising or unapproved purposes. From the July 2026 policy update, account verification via phone call is no longer an approved READ_CALL_LOG use case (use the Digital Credentials API or SMS Retriever instead).
why_it_matters: Android will technically let you send a message without a tap, but only if your app has displaced the user's default messaging app — an adoption bar almost no assistant clears.

title: NotificationListenerService: real ambient awareness, under restricted-permission rules
what_is_allowed: With user-granted notification access, an app can read the full current set of notifications on the device, including metadata and attached PendingIntents — which is the richest passive signal of what is happening in a person's life that any third-party app can legitimately obtain on either platform.
what_is_forbidden: Access is not a runtime permission: the user must grant it on a dedicated Settings screen. Google Play treats it as a restricted permission with additional requirements — request it only for a genuine core feature, never harvest or transmit notification content, and never manipulate users into granting it. Misuse falls under the Permissions and APIs that Access Sensitive Information policy.
why_it_matters: This asymmetry is the strongest argument for building the proactive product Android-first: the sensing layer exists there and has no iOS equivalent.

title: Background execution: typed foreground services, denied-by-default exact alarms, Android 17 audio hardening
what_is_allowed: Declared foreground service types (Android 14+) for legitimate ongoing work. Calendar and alarm-clock apps may declare `USE_EXACT_ALARM`, a normal permission granted at install. Other apps may request `SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM`, which is denied by default from Android 14 and must be granted by the user in Settings. WorkManager handles deferrable background work.
what_is_forbidden: Geofencing was REMOVED as an approved foreground-service use case in the April 15, 2026 Play policy update — developers must use the Geofence API instead. Starting a foreground service from the background is heavily restricted. Android 17 background audio hardening requires a while-in-use-capable foreground service for background audio focus/volume changes (waived only for exact-alarm holders acting on USAGE_ALARM streams). Apps holding exact-alarm permission that continue alarms in the background must declare foreground service types.
why_it_matters: Android gives you more background rope than iOS, but each strand now requires a declared, policy-reviewed justification — 'my agent is thinking' is not one of them.

title: Broad contacts access is being retired in favour of the Contact Picker
what_is_allowed: Using the Android Contact Picker to obtain the specific contacts the user chooses, per interaction.
what_is_forbidden: Per the April 15, 2026 policy announcement, apps requiring broad contact access must migrate to the Android Contact Picker for safer, more limited data access. Location policy tightened in the same update: the location button is now the recommended minimum scope for precise location. Minimum 30 days from April 15, 2026 to comply.
why_it_matters: A proactive assistant cannot assume a full address book on Android any more than on iOS — relationship graphs must be built from what the user hands over, one picker at a time.

title: Live Updates / Notification.ProgressStyle — Android's proactive surface, largely unclaimed
what_is_allowed: Android 16 introduces Live Updates: persistent promoted notifications that pin to the top of the shade, show a status-bar chip, and render glanceable real-time progress on the lock screen, built on the new `Notification.ProgressStyle` template with progress segments and points. Intended for ride share, delivery, and navigation.
what_is_forbidden: Like iOS Live Activities, the surface presumes a real ongoing, time-sensitive activity rather than ambient assistant chatter. Adoption is thin — Google Maps was effectively the only implementation for most of the first year, with Wallet flight tracking added later, and third-party uptake is described as a ghost town compared to Apple's.
why_it_matters: An uncontested, high-salience proactive surface on Android is available to whoever bothers to ship on it first.

title: Gemini Personal Intelligence has no third-party developer API
what_is_allowed: Since January 14, 2026, the Gemini app can draw personal context from a user's Google apps (Gmail, Photos, Search, YouTube) with permission, across web, Android and iOS, and connect to a short list of named third-party apps including WhatsApp, Spotify, Canva, Samsung Gallery and Samsung Notes.
what_is_forbidden: Google has not announced public API access to Personal Intelligence. The deep personal-data integration is limited to the consumer Gemini app; the Gemini API exposes the model, not the user's personal context. Third-party apps cannot read the personal graph Gemini builds, and inclusion in the connected-apps list is a business-development outcome, not a developer self-serve integration.
why_it_matters: On both platforms the personal-context layer is owned by the OS vendor's own assistant and is not resold to third parties — so your assistant must build its own memory from scratch.

title: No first-party persistent personal-memory API exists for third-party apps
what_is_allowed: Apps may build and store their own memory — Apple's Foundation Models adds 'Dynamic Profiles' to change how models interact with an app on the fly, and Google shipped memory import for Gemini in March 2026 letting users upload structured personal context that persists across conversations. Third-party memory infrastructure (Mem0, Zep, Supermemory via MCP) is mature and available.
what_is_forbidden: Neither Apple nor Google exposes the user's cross-app personal memory to third-party app code. Apple states plainly that third-party apps never see other apps' data and that personal-context processing stays on-device or in PCC. Dynamic Profiles configures model behaviour, not user memory; Gemini memory import is a consumer feature of the Gemini app.
why_it_matters: Personal memory is a moat you must dig yourself, and it can only be filled with data the user explicitly grants you — which makes the grant flow the actual product.

title: OSWorld 2.0: best frontier agent completes 20.6% of long-horizon real tasks
what_is_allowed: On the original OSWorld benchmark, computer-use agents rose from ~12% success (April 2024) to roughly 85% by June 2026 — short, well-scoped GUI tasks are close to solved.
what_is_forbidden: On OSWorld 2.0 — 108 long-horizon workflows whose median task takes a human ~1.6 hours and requires an average of 318 tool calls (vs ~30 in OSWorld 1.0) — Claude Opus 4.8 with maximum thinking completes only 20.6% of tasks at a 54.8% partial score at 500 steps, and GPT-5.5 plateaus near 13%. The paper's conclusion: 'Current agents are still far from professional-level computer use.'
why_it_matters: The gap between 85% on short tasks and 20.6% on real multi-hour workflows is the whole risk profile of shipping an autonomous assistant to consumers.

title: AndroidWorld is saturated at >90%; MobileWorld drops the best framework to 51.7%
what_is_allowed: AndroidWorld (116 programmatic tasks across 20 real Android apps) is saturated — state-of-the-art agentic frameworks now exceed 90% success on its leaderboard. Mid-tier published systems: MobileUse 62.9%, K²-Agent 76.7%.
what_is_forbidden: MobileWorld (201 tasks, 20 apps, agent-user interactive and MCP-augmented) shows the real picture: the best agentic FRAMEWORK reaches 51.7% and the best END-TO-END model reaches 20.9%. The benchmark authors built it precisely because AndroidWorld's saturation 'fundamentally limits the ability to distinguish incremental improvements from genuine breakthroughs'.
why_it_matters: Roughly half of realistic multi-step phone tasks fail even in a lab with full device control — before any platform policy is applied.

title: Published failure modes: agents guess instead of asking, and lose track mid-task
what_is_allowed: Agents reliably execute basic GUI control; the OSWorld 2.0 authors note the bottleneck is reasoning and state management, not clicking.
what_is_forbidden: OSWorld 2.0 verbatim: agents 'lose track of constraints, miss information that arrives mid-task, guess rather than ask the user, and skip verification, struggling most when a task hinges on hidden state they must recover.' MobileWorld identifies five modes: (1) ambiguity — agents hallucinate plausible but wrong information rather than seeking clarification, affecting 22.4% of tasks; (2) long MCP tool outputs overflowing context; (3) no mechanism to track completed subtasks, producing repeated modifications and destructive action loops; (4) weak multi-step logical and numerical reasoning; (5) failure to ground actions in actual device time/location without explicit prompting, causing scheduling errors.
why_it_matters: The dominant failure is confidently doing the wrong thing without asking — which is precisely the failure a consumer will never forgive in an assistant acting on their behalf.

title: On-device models are invocation-scoped, not continuously running
what_is_allowed: Full on-device LLM inference with vision input is real and free at the margin on current hardware — Apple's Foundation Models framework on iOS, Gemini Nano via AICore / ML Kit GenAI on Android. Work can be triggered by system events: HealthKit background delivery, App Intent invocation with iOS 27 LongRunningIntent extension, WorkManager, or a typed foreground service.
what_is_forbidden: Neither platform provides a way for a model to run continuously in the background reasoning about the user's day on its own initiative. iOS grants at most 1 refresh + 10 processing tasks, all opportunistic and suppressed after force-quit; Android requires a declared foreground service type with a user-visible notification and a policy-approved justification. Every unit of compute is downstream of either a user action or a system event.
why_it_matters: Proactivity on a stock phone must be architected as event-triggered inference with persisted state between wakes — an always-thinking daemon is not a shippable design on either platform.
